one_liner: Rust crate that parses JSON to a simdjson-format tape on Apple Silicon GPUs (Metal); beats C++ simdjson above ~4-5 MiB.
what_it_does: metal-json parses a whole standard (RFC 8259) JSON document on the Apple GPU with Metal compute kernels. It returns a `Document` that holds a 64-bit tape in simdjson's layout plus a buffer of unescaped strings, and the CPU reads both in place from unified memory. The API is its own Rust interface, not a simdjson binding: you build a reusable `Parser` and call `parse`, `parse_aligned` or `parse_file` (or the zero-copy `unsafe parse_file_mmap`). You then navigate with `Value::get`/`at`/`entries`/`elements`/`as_*`, or deserialize into typed structs through the optional `serde` feature. It validates the full grammar and UTF-8 strictly, types numbers i64 -> u64 -> f64 the way simdjson does, and returns errors as values with byte offsets.
how_it_is_fast: Stage 1 ports simdjson's bitmap tricks to Metal: backslash-run escape detection and a prefix-XOR in-string mask. Each GPU thread handles one 64-byte word using `uint2` bitmaps, because 64-bit operations are emulated on Apple's 32-bit ALUs, and state crosses chunk boundaries through reduce->spine->apply scans rather than decoupled look-back. Brackets are matched without a stack: a stable LSD counting sort of the structural characters by nesting depth puts each open/close pair next to each other, which also yields separator context and child counts. Apple GPUs have no fp64, so numbers use an integer-only Eisel-Lemire port; rare hard roundings and strings over 16 KiB are sent to CPU fixup lists. Unified memory shares both the input (`MTLBuffer bytesNoCopy`) and the output tape with the CPU without copies, and a buffer pool makes steady-state parses free of large allocations.
when_to_use: Single JSON documents of roughly 8 MiB and up (dumps, exports, big API payloads) parsed on an Apple Silicon Mac. The author measured 1.34x over C++ simdjson at 8 MiB, rising to 2.06-2.71x at 100-512 MiB on twitter-shaped data.
Number-dense documents such as coordinate/GeoJSON arrays: canada.json (2.1 MiB) already parsed 1.42x faster than simdjson, below the twitter crossover.
Throughput-bound batch jobs that keep one `Parser` alive, so the Metal device, pipeline states and pooled buffers stay warm across parses.

Rust code that needs a fully materialized tape of a huge file (random access, O(1) subtree skips) rather than streaming extraction. In the same report it was about 3.5x faster than Rust simd-json at 512 MiB (7.51 vs 2.16 GB/s) and 1.35x faster at 4 MiB.
when_not_to_use: Small documents or per-request latency paths. Every parse pays about 0.5-0.9 ms of fixed dispatch/sync overhead: simdjson was about 8x faster on twitter.json (0.6 MiB), about 3x faster at 1 MiB, and 2.3x faster on citm_catalog (1.6 MiB).

Anything other than macOS on Apple Silicon: there is no Linux, Windows, x86 or discrete-GPU path. The only non-GPU backend is the slow `cpu-reference` oracle (0.23-0.36 GB/s). Inputs are also capped at 4 GiB - 65 bytes because tape and token indices are u32.

Typed deserialization of mid-size payloads. On a ~4 MiB corpus, serde_json straight into structs was about 2.5x faster end-to-end than metal-json's serde path (~972 vs ~384 MiB/s, both borrowed), because the GPU always builds the whole tape before any type-driven work.

Workloads where CPU cores can run in parallel (many documents, NDJSON). The baseline was a single simdjson DOM parse on one core (per the vendored simdjson.h, its threading applies only to parse_many lookahead). Multi-core CPU parsing was not compared.

Production dependencies that need a maintainer. The code was written over about two days in June 2026 and v0.1.0 has 83 crates.io downloads. Human commits stopped on 2026-06-15; only Renovate bumps have landed since. Hosted CI does not run the GPU kernels because GitHub's paravirtual Metal compiler crashes, so GPU tests run only on the author's hardware.

integration.dependencies: objc2, objc2-foundation, objc2-metal, block2, dispatch2, memmap2, thiserror; optional serde. The default build also needs the Xcode Metal toolchain (`xcrun metal`) unless the `runtime-shaders` feature is enabled.
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.95 (edition 2024; the repo pins 1.96.0). The default ahead-of-time shader build needs the Xcode Metal toolchain; `--features runtime-shaders` compiles MSL at runtime instead. Minimum macOS version is not documented.
integration.platforms: macOS on Apple Silicon only (Metal GPU with unified memory); benchmarked only on an M5 Max
integration.thread_safety: `Parser` is not Send/Sync (its GPU state is shared through `Rc`, and its docs call the Send/Sync story unfinished), so use one `Parser` per thread. `Document` is Send + Sync, and its buffers return to a Mutex-guarded pool on drop. Concurrent parsing from several parsers is neither documented nor benchmarked.

gotchas: `Value::get` and `Value::at` scan the container's direct children linearly (nested containers are skipped in O(1)), so indexing a big array in a loop is quadratic; iterate with `elements()`/`entries()` instead. `len()` is O(1) except for containers with 16,777,215 or more children, where the saturated count forces a walk.

Duplicate keys stay on the tape and resolve three different ways: `Value::get` returns the first, serde into a map keeps the last, and serde into a struct fails with a 'duplicate field' error. Integers beyond u64 are stored as f64 (simdjson parity), so i128/u128 targets reject them, unlike serde_json.

The buffer pool grows to the high-water mark and never shrinks: after one huge parse, that memory stays held until the `Parser` and all its `Document`s are dropped. `parse` and `parse_file` copy the input once. Only `parse_aligned` (caller-held `AlignedInput`) and the `unsafe parse_file_mmap` are zero-copy, and the mmap path can SIGBUS if the file is truncated mid-parse.

The tape mirrors simdjson's layout except for string-buffer offsets, which are allocated by raw (escaped) length and leave zero-filled gaps, so code that walks simdjson's dense string buffer will not work unchanged. For distributed binaries, prefer `--features runtime-shaders`: the default build panics in build.rs when `xcrun metal` is missing. GPU wall times jitter up to 4x from power-state ramping, so benchmark with warm-up and medians.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over simdjson only for single documents above roughly 5-8 MiB on an Apple Silicon Mac, when you want a full simdjson-style tape from Rust; below that, simdjson is faster and portable. Rust simd-json likewise beat it at 0.6-1.6 MiB (except number-heavy canada) but trailed about 3.5x at 512 MiB. For huge single records on multi-core CPUs, Pison (reported 3.1-5.4x over simdjson with 4-8 threads) and the query-oriented JSONSki are the portable alternatives, but neither was benchmarked against metal-json.
verified_claims_summary: The author's bench report (2026-06-12) times parse-to-tape plus an identical stats walk for metal-json against vendored C++ simdjson v4.6.4 on one Apple M5 Max (128 GiB, macOS 26.5.1). simdjson ran its single-document DOM parser, built with -O3 -mcpu=native through the Rust cc crate (compiler version not stated), and both parsers were checked for bit-identical stats before timing. metal-json won 1.34x at 8 MiB rising to 2.71x at 512 MiB (7.51 vs 2.77 GB/s) on twitter-template expansions, and 1.42x on canada (2.1 MiB). It lost below about 4.3 MiB (0.12x at 0.6 MiB, 0.44x on citm_catalog), and non-twitter shapes were measured only at their small canonical sizes.
status_note: Published as crate 0.1.0 (MIT; the README's 'MIT OR Apache-2.0' contradicts LICENSE and Cargo.toml); since 2026-06-15 only Renovate dependency bumps have landed (latest 2026-09-21) and a v0.1.1 release PR sits unmerged, so treat it as a finished, heavily tested experiment rather than an actively developed library.
